chunks: "If the eye is too small, the receiver has less margin, so noise and jitter can push a sample across the decision threshold and it reads the wrong bit. That's a bit error.
Because noise is roughly Gaussian, the error rate goes up very steeply as the eye closes: a modest shrink can turn one error in 10 to the 12 bits into one in 10 to the 6 .
In a real system you see CRC errors, retransmissions, link retraining or fallback to a lower speed, or in the worst case the link doesn't come up at all.

To put a number on it, the usual metrics are the eye height and eye width, in millivolts and picoseconds or as a fraction of the unit interval; the Q factor, which is the separation between the signal levels divided by the sum of the noise standard deviations; and ultimately the bit error rate.
They're connected: BER equals 1 over 2 erfc (Q over square root of 2) , so Q of 7 corresponds to about 10 to the -12 and Q of 6 to about 10 to the -9 .
You'd also look at a bathtub curve, which plots BER versus sampling position across the UI, and at mask margin for compliance.
If the eye is small, you fix the causes: equalize the loss, reduce reflections, jitter and noise."
